question: How can linear models be recast in a dual, kernel form, and how does that lead to kernel construction, RBF networks, Nadaraya-Watson regression and Gaussian processes?

Rules and examples for constructing valid kernels incl. generative and Fisher kernels (6.2)
RBF networks and Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression (6.3)
Gaussian processes for regression and classification, hyperparameter learning, ARD, link to neural networks (6.4)

limits: No empirical benchmarks: the chapter has only synthetic illustrations (sinusoidal data, a 3-input ARD set, a 2-class 2-D set) and gives no sample sizes beyond N=100 in the ARD example.
Support vector machines and sparse kernel machines are deferred to Chapter 7; this chapter has no max-margin treatment.
GP cost is O(N^3); approximation schemes are only cited (Gibbs 1997; Tresp 2001; Smola and Bartlett 2001; Williams and Seeger 2001; Csato and Opper 2002; Seeger et al. 2003).
Log likelihood of GP hyperparameters is nonconvex with multiple maxima; fully Bayesian marginalisation over theta is intractable.
GP classification integral (6.76) is intractable; needs sampling, variational, EP or Laplace approximations.
Neural-network GP limit loses shared hidden units across outputs.
2006 text: no mention of deep kernels, random features or scalable GPs.
practices: Use the kernel trick: if x enters only through scalar products, replace them with a kernel (p.292).
Check kernel validity by positive semidefiniteness of the Gram matrix, not nonnegative entries (p.295).
Build new kernels from valid ones with closure rules (6.13)-(6.22) (p.296).
For RBF networks, pick centres by random subset, orthogonal least squares or K-means (p.301).
Normalise basis functions to avoid regions where all are small (p.300).
Learn GP hyperparameters by maximising log likelihood with conjugate gradients, and use ARD to discard irrelevant inputs (pp.311-313).
For GP classification, find the posterior mode by Newton-Raphson/IRLS and use the Laplace approximation (pp.316-317).

methods that involve storing the entire training set in order to make predictions for future data points
if an algorithm uses x only through scalar products, replace the scalar product with another kernel
k(x,x')=k(x-x'), invariant to translations in input space
k(x,x')=k(||x-x'||), depends only on distance between arguments
K=Phi Phi^T, N x N symmetric with K_nm = k(x_n,x_m)
k(x,x')=g(theta,x)^T F^-1 g(theta,x') with Fisher score g=grad_theta ln p(x|theta)
kernel regression y(x)=sum_n k(x,x_n) t_n with normalised kernel (6.45)-(6.46)
a probability distribution over functions y(x) such that the values of y(x) at an arbitrary set of points jointly have a Gaussian distribution
a separate precision parameter eta_i per input in the kernel, optimised by maximum likelihood so irrelevant inputs get small eta_i
